dicas.texto: Você está indo bem! Lembre-se: o denominador indica em quantas partes cada unidade (de 0 a 1, de 1 a 2) deve ser dividida. Como você marcaria 10 partes se cada unidade só tem 6?
Tente dividir cada unidade (0-1 e 1-2) em 6 partes iguais. Depois, conte 10 dessas marcações começando do zero.
Você está quase lá! Ao dividir cada unidade em 6, você terá 12 marcações no total até o número 2. Onde o 10º tracinho se localiza?
Conte os tracinhos um a um: 1/6, 2/6... até chegar no 10/6. O ponto que você encontrar está na mesma altura que o 12/9 da Linha 1?
Frações equivalentes ocupam exatamente o mesmo ponto na reta numérica. Se os pontos estão em lugares diferentes, o que isso nos diz sobre a igualdade?
Observe a distância de cada ponto em relação ao número 1. Eles estão na mesma posição?
O ponto 12/9 está em um lugar e o 10/6 está em outro. O sinal de igualdade é apropriado para valores diferentes?
Como as posições são diferentes, selecione o símbolo de 'diferente' (≠) no seletor.

dicas.texto: Look for a number that divides both the numerator and denominator evenly.
Divide the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor.
Both 12 and 9 can be divided by 3 without leaving a remainder.
Divide 12 by 3 for the numerator and divide 9 by 3 for the denominator.
The denominator tells how many equal intervals make up one whole.
Read the denominator of the fraction that belongs on Line 2 and enter that number.
For 10/6, focus on the number below the fraction bar.
Enter the denominator from 10/6 in the field, then confirm the division of the line.
The numerator tells how many equal intervals to count from zero.
Start at 0 and move one sixth at a time until you reach the numerator count.
Count ten sixth-sized intervals, passing the mark for one whole.
From zero, count ten intervals of the size created on Line 2 and place the marker at that position.
The numerator is the number above the fraction bar.
Read the number of intervals counted from zero and enter it in the numerator field.
The point on Line 2 was reached after counting ten equal intervals.
Enter the number that counts the marked intervals above the denominator 6.
Equivalent fractions mark exactly the same position on a number line.
Compare the two marked positions before choosing the comparison sign.
One point represents 4/3 and the other represents 5/3; they do not coincide.
Choose the sign that means the two values are different rather than the sign that means they are equal.
Use both number lines to confirm whether the two fractions have the same value.
Check the simplified form of the first fraction and the marked form of the second fraction.
The first fraction simplifies to 4/3, while the second fraction remains represented by ten sixths.
Verify the not-equal sign and the numerator displayed over denominator 6, then complete the activity.

hints.message: Look for a number that divides both the numerator and denominator evenly.
Divide the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor.
Both 12 and 9 can be divided by 3 without leaving a remainder.
Divide 12 by 3 for the numerator and divide 9 by 3 for the denominator.

nodes.description: Divide Line 2 into equal parts for the denominator of 10/6.
nodes.instruction: Divide Line 2 into equal parts for the denominator of 10/6.

hints.message: The denominator tells how many equal intervals make up one whole.
Read the denominator of the fraction that belongs on Line 2 and enter that number.
For 10/6, focus on the number below the fraction bar.
Enter the denominator from 10/6 in the field, then confirm the division of the line.

misconceptions.description: O aluno usa o denominador da primeira fração para a segunda por falta de compreensão da independência das escalas
misconceptions.feedback: Check the fraction for Line 2. Its denominator is 6, not the denominator from the first fraction.

misconceptions.description: O aluno conta os tracinhos desenhados no papel em vez dos espaços entre eles
misconceptions.feedback: The denominator counts equal intervals, not just the interior marks. Count the spaces created on the line.

nodes.description: Mark the position represented by 10/6 on Line 2.
nodes.instruction: Mark the position represented by 10/6 on Line 2.

hints.message: The numerator tells how many equal intervals to count from zero.
Start at 0 and move one sixth at a time until you reach the numerator count.
Count ten sixth-sized intervals, passing the mark for one whole.
From zero, count ten intervals of the size created on Line 2 and place the marker at that position.

nodes.description: Enter the numerator of the fraction shown for Line 2.
nodes.instruction: Enter the numerator of the fraction shown for Line 2.

hints.message: The numerator is the number above the fraction bar.
Read the number of intervals counted from zero and enter it in the numerator field.
The point on Line 2 was reached after counting ten equal intervals.
Enter the number that counts the marked intervals above the denominator 6.

nodes.description: Set the comparison sign between the two fractions to show they are not equivalent.
nodes.instruction: Set the comparison sign between the two fractions to show they are not equivalent.

hints.message: Equivalent fractions mark exactly the same position on a number line.
Compare the two marked positions before choosing the comparison sign.
One point represents 4/3 and the other represents 5/3; they do not coincide.
Choose the sign that means the two values are different rather than the sign that means they are equal.

misconceptions.description: O aluno tenta aplicar operações aritméticas nas partes da fração para justificar a equivalência
misconceptions.feedback: Adding numerators and denominators is not a valid way to test equivalence. Compare the positions or simplify the fractions instead.

nodes.description: Confirm the final comparison after completing both number lines.
nodes.instruction: Confirm the final comparison after completing both number lines.

hints.message: Use both number lines to confirm whether the two fractions have the same value.
Check the simplified form of the first fraction and the marked form of the second fraction.
The first fraction simplifies to 4/3, while the second fraction remains represented by ten sixths.
Verify the not-equal sign and the numerator displayed over denominator 6, then complete the activity.
